summary: Jethro brings Zipporah and Moses’ sons to the mountain, hears of Israel’s deliverance, blesses Yahweh, and shares a sacrificial meal with Aaron and the elders. Seeing Moses judge disputes alone all day, he warns that both Moses and the people will wear out and advises selecting trustworthy judges for ordinary cases while Moses retains the difficult ones; Moses follows that advice.
whyItMatters: A Midianite family member recognizes the rescue and contributes practical wisdom to Israel’s emerging community. Shared judgment addresses the people’s access to decisions as well as Moses’ limited capacity.

context.author: Exodus names no writer of the finished book, though it depicts Moses writing particular words. Later tradition ascribes the Torah to him; its composition remains debated.
context.audience: Israel is addressed through its story of rescue, covenant, and worship; this chapter names no narrower first audience.
context.date: The book gives a relative story sequence but no secure external year for the events. The dating and formation of its finished text remain debated.
context.setting: Israel’s wilderness camp at the mountain of God, especially Moses’ tent and the place where people wait for judgments.
context.literaryForm: Family reunion and praise followed by observed administrative strain, counsel, implementation, and departure.

before.text: Israel has received water at Rephidim and fought Amalek, with the victory marked by an altar. Jethro hears of the journey and comes with Moses’ family.

here.text: Jethro responds to the deliverance, then sees an exhausting judging practice and proposes qualified helpers. Moses appoints them to judge routine cases while he handles difficult ones.

after.text: Israel reaches Sinai; Moses relays a covenant proposal, the people answer, and they prepare for a dangerous encounter at the mountain.

outline.heading: Jethro brings Moses’ family
outline.note: The Midianite priest arrives with Zipporah and the two named sons.

outline.heading: Report, praise, and shared meal
outline.note: Moses tells the deliverance story; Jethro blesses Yahweh and offers sacrifice.

outline.heading: The burden of judging alone
outline.note: People stand around Moses all day, and Jethro says the arrangement wears everyone down.

outline.heading: A system of qualified judges proposed
outline.note: Moses should teach and refer routine cases to trustworthy leaders while hearing hard cases.

outline.heading: Counsel enacted and Jethro departs
outline.note: Moses appoints leaders, shares the work, and sends Jethro on his way.

keyVerses.text: Now I know that Yahweh is greater than all gods because of the way that they treated people arrogantly.”
keyVerses.why: Jethro openly credits Yahweh with deliverance and makes a claim about the gods.

keyVerses.text: You will surely wear away, both you, and this people that is with you; for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to perform it yourself alone.
keyVerses.why: His criticism focuses on exhaustion for both Moses and the waiting people.

keyVerses.text: Moreover you shall provide out of all the people able men which fear God: men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.
keyVerses.why: The proposed judges are to be able, truthful, reverent, and resistant to unjust gain.

questions.question: Who comes to Moses with Jethro?
questions.answer: Jethro brings Moses’ wife Zipporah and their sons Gershom and Eliezer to the wilderness camp. The text says Moses had sent Zipporah away but does not explain when or why that happened.

questions.question: What do the sons’ names recall?
questions.answer: Gershom is tied to Moses living as a foreigner, and Eliezer to his father’s God helping him escape Pharaoh’s sword. The explanations place displacement and deliverance within Moses’ family record.

questions.question: How does Jethro respond to Moses’ report?
questions.answer: He rejoices in Yahweh’s goodness to Israel, blesses Yahweh for deliverance, and brings offerings. Aaron and the elders then share a meal with him before God.

questions.question: What status does the text give Jethro as he praises Yahweh and advises Moses?
questions.answer: Jethro is called a priest of Midian and Moses’ father-in-law, so the advisor comes from outside Israel. He blesses Yahweh, shares a sacrificial meal with Israel’s elders, and offers counsel that Moses receives.

questions.question: What problem does Jethro see with Moses’ current work?
questions.answer: Moses judges cases from morning to evening while people stand waiting around him. Jethro says the work is too heavy for one person and will wear out both the judge and those seeking decisions.

questions.question: What are the “hard cases” under the new arrangement?
questions.answer: They are matters the selected judges bring to Moses while deciding smaller disputes themselves. The chapter does not list those cases, but it clearly distinguishes shared routine work from questions referred upward.

questions.question: What protects the proposed judges from using office for gain?
questions.answer: Jethro calls for able people who fear God, are truthful, and hate unjust gain. Under his proposal such judges handle routine matters, while the difficult cases continue to reach Moses.

questions.question: Does Moses merely hear the advice or implement it?
questions.answer: He listens, selects able people from Israel, and sets them over groups of different sizes. The new judges decide ordinary cases, while difficult matters continue to reach Moses.

glossary.def: The Midianite priest and father-in-law who visits Moses and advises him on judging disputes.
The divine requirements Moses says he teaches when deciding matters among the people.
The self-serving profit that Jethro says appointed judges must reject.
